CARES PostgreSQL Technical Decisions (Preparation)

Status: Documentation and technical decision preparation only (NOT IMPLEMENTED, NOT TESTED). This document consolidates unresolved technical issues, options, proposed recommendations, dependencies, and validation requirements to support formal PostgreSQL schema/security design review. It does not create schema/DDL/migrations, implement controls, or resolve owner/commercial/privacy/legal/security/operational approvals.

Sources reviewed: ARCHITECTURE.md, DATA_ARCHITECTURE.md, SECURITY_ARCHITECTURE.md, ARCHITECTURE_DECISION_PACKAGE_FINAL_CORRECTIONS.md, adr/0006-atomic-per-tenant-asset-licensing.md, ARCHITECTURE_CROSS_DOCUMENT_CONSISTENCY_REVIEW.md.

Decision register

Decision ID Topic Status Summary recommendation (technical, proposed)
TD-001 PostgreSQL version and verified transaction-context binding mechanism Proposed Select a supported PostgreSQL version and implement protected verifier-written, transaction-bound context bound to backend/session transaction identity with explicit cleanup/fail-closed semantics; do not use custom GUCs as authorization source
TD-002 Tenant assertion verification, nonce lifecycle, and trusted helper interfaces Proposed Hardened SECURITY DEFINER verifier performs full assertion validation and nonce consumption; narrow helpers expose only required decisions/values; non-authoritative diagnostics only outside authz path
TD-003 Logical database roles, ownership, grants, and SECURITY DEFINER boundaries Proposed Enforce logical roles cares_api_runtime, cares_ingest_runtime, cares_worker_runtime, cares_migration, cares_maintenance with least privilege, NOLOGIN/controlled definer ownership, fixed search_path, minimal grants, and no runtime ownership/bypass
TD-004 RLS policy catalog and FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY applicability Proposed Restrictive tenant boundary + permissive/action-scope gates using verified context helpers; enable RLS and apply FORCE RLS where ownership/role design permits; explicitly design UPDATE/SELECT/RETURNING visibility
TD-005 Identity binding and fingerprint alias schema semantics Proposed Reconciled model: canonical asset, stable asset_data_source binding, stable source_device_key_id, versioned source_device_fingerprint_alias; tenant-scoped uniqueness, overlap/rotation/collision/migration without duplicates or licensed-usage inflation
TD-006 Operation-by-operation transaction-boundary map Proposed Define atomic commit boundaries per operation for business state, idempotency/result, audit/lifecycle/licensing/evidence records, and outbox records; fail closed on partial/ambiguous outcomes
TD-007 Idempotency ledger scope and unknown-commit recovery Proposed Separate ingestion event_receipt, licensing/identity operation idempotency ledger, and outbox attempt/replay records; durable request-hash/result semantics and reconciliation for unknown commit/timeout/retry
TD-008 Outbox scope, delivery ambiguity, reconciliation, and replay Proposed Distinguish event-processing outbox from controlled/external-side-effect outbox; use leases/fencing, cumulative attempts, generation-scoped replay controls, delivery_unknown safety state, reconciliation evidence/authorization before ambiguous replay
TD-009 Evidence storage metadata, custody, and controlled transitions Proposed Immutable evidence metadata/objects with append-only custody sequencing/hash linkage; protected transaction-bound single-use authorization for controlled transitions (not GUC), atomic state/custody/authorization handling; recognize DB hash-chain trust-boundary limits

TD-001 — PostgreSQL version and verified transaction-context binding mechanism

  • Problem statement: CARES requires tenant isolation/RLS and authorization decisions to rely on protected, verifier-written, transaction-bound verified context. Custom PostgreSQL GUCs are explicitly prohibited as authentication/authorization sources, but the exact PostgreSQL version, transaction-binding identifier/primitive, and cleanup/anti-reuse mechanism are not selected.
  • Security or correctness implications: Incorrect binding (or fallback to GUC/session state) can enable cross-tenant access, context replay, pool/session bleed, backend PID/transaction identifier reuse authorization, and fail-open behavior.
  • Available technical options:
    1. Security-internal verifier-written transaction context table keyed to current backend and transaction identity with narrow helper reads and explicit cleanup/binding checks (preferred conceptual direction in final corrections).
    2. Transaction-local temp table populated by verifier/definer code (simpler lifetime, weaker boundary against same-session untrusted SQL/tampering depending on model).
    3. Opaque handle in non-authoritative GUC/session variable + protected lookup record (handle not proof; must validate against current binding/protected record every use).
    4. Per-statement external verification only (high latency/complexity; unsuitable as primary RLS source).
  • Advantages and disadvantages:
    • Option 1: Pros: strong non-GUC authorization source, auditable boundary, explicit claims/nonce linkage possible. Cons: requires careful binding semantics, helper overhead, cleanup/anti-reuse design, and PostgreSQL-version-specific validation.
    • Option 2: Pros: natural transaction scope. Cons: same-session tamper risk/visibility concerns; less robust as a security boundary.
    • Option 3: Pros: can avoid exposing claims in GUC. Cons: added complexity; easy to misuse if handle treated as authority.
    • Option 4: Pros: separation of crypto verification concerns. Cons: operationally complex, hard to make atomic with DB RLS decisions.
  • Recommended option, with technical justification: Option 1 (Proposed). It best satisfies the documented requirement that authorization helpers read protected verifier-written state rather than mutable caller/session configuration, and supports fail-closed binding/cleanup validation.
  • Dependencies and assumptions: Selected/supported PostgreSQL major/minor version; availability and semantics of transaction/backend identifiers and required features; pooling/reset behavior; security-internal schema permissions; hardened verifier implementation. Assumes no reliance on untrusted GUC values for allow/deny.
  • Validation required: Production-equivalent PostgreSQL tests for GUC forgery resistance, pool/session bleed, PID/transaction reuse, cleanup/rollback behavior, helper privilege boundaries, fail-closed missing/invalid/expired context, and RLS enforcement under concurrent pooled connections.
  • Status: Proposed.

TD-002 — Tenant assertion verification, nonce lifecycle, and trusted helper interfaces

  • Problem statement: The system needs a trustworthy way to establish tenant/principal/scope context per transaction/job, including signature/claim validation, replay prevention, and minimal helper interfaces consumable by RLS/policies and controlled procedures.
  • Security or correctness implications: Weak verification or nonce handling enables tenant spoofing, replay, scope escalation, stale-context reuse, and unauthorized cross-tenant data access or evidence/licensing actions.
  • Available technical options:
    1. Hardened SECURITY DEFINER verifier function(s) that validate canonical claims/signature/issuer/audience/tenant/principal/scopes/expiry/skew/request or job binding, consume nonce, and write protected context atomically.
    2. Application-only verification with database trusting application-provided context (insufficient for DB-enforced tenant isolation).
    3. Split verification: external/auth service verifies assertion and DB verifier records only DB-binding proof (possible but more moving parts).
  • Advantages and disadvantages:
    • Option 1: Pros: single DB-visible trust boundary for RLS helpers; can atomically bind nonce/context to transaction. Cons: requires strict definer hardening, key/signature design decisions, and careful interface minimization.
    • Option 2: Pros: simpler DB layer. Cons: does not meet defense-in-depth/RLS trust requirements; unacceptable risk.
    • Option 3: Pros: crypto/service separation. Cons: increased protocol complexity and failure modes; must still prevent forged DB binding.
  • Recommended option, with technical justification: Option 1 (Proposed), possibly with external support services only if DB-recorded binding/proof remains verifier-controlled and fail-closed. Aligns with SECURITY_ARCHITECTURE.md and ARCHITECTURE_DECISION_PACKAGE_FINAL_CORRECTIONS.md.
  • Dependencies and assumptions: Assertion format/canonicalization and signature algorithm; issuer/audience/key distribution and rotation/revocation; nonce storage/TTL/cleanup; trusted time/skew policy; request/job binding semantics; TD-001 binding mechanism; TD-003 definer/role boundaries.
  • Validation required: Positive/negative cryptographic and DB tests for invalid signature/issuer/audience/tenant/principal/scope/expiry/skew/nonce replay, missing context, helper output minimization (no full context leakage), and atomic nonce-consume+context-bind behavior.
  • Status: Proposed.

TD-003 — Logical database roles, ownership, grants, and SECURITY DEFINER boundaries

  • Problem statement: Reconciled documents require normalized logical role separation and strict boundaries for ordinary runtime roles, migration/maintenance roles, and security-critical definer functions/helpers.
  • Security or correctness implications: Over-privileged roles, unsafe definer ownership/search paths, or direct access to security-internal tables can bypass RLS, forge context/authorizations, corrupt evidence/licensing state, or create un-auditable privileged operations.
  • Available technical options:
    1. Granular logical roles + security-internal schema ownership by controlled NOLOGIN owners + hardened SECURITY DEFINER helpers with fixed search_path and minimal EXECUTE grants (reconciled direction).
    2. Single runtime role plus coarse admin role (simpler operations, high privilege concentration).
    3. Per-feature fine-grained roles beyond the five logical roles (more granular, higher operational complexity).
  • Advantages and disadvantages:
    • Option 1: Pros: aligns least privilege with API/ingest/worker/migration/maintenance responsibilities; supports defense in depth. Cons: requires careful grant/ownership matrix and testing.
    • Option 2: Pros: simpler to configure initially. Cons: conflicts with reconciled security posture and increases blast radius.
    • Option 3: Pros: potentially tighter isolation. Cons: complexity may delay correct implementation; not required by current reconciliation.
  • Recommended option, with technical justification: Option 1 (Proposed). Preserve the five logical roles and enforce explicit prohibitions for ordinary runtime roles (no SUPERUSER/BYPASSRLS, no ownership of protected tables/policies/security-critical functions, no direct security-internal table mutation except approved narrow interfaces).
  • Dependencies and assumptions: TD-001/TD-002 helper interfaces; schema/table ownership design; extension/maintenance procedures; controlled break-glass model (owner/security decision). Assumes production-equivalent non-owner role testing.
  • Validation required: Grant/ownership audits, SECURITY DEFINER hardening review, search-path/function-resolution tests, privilege-escalation negative tests, and RLS tests under exact runtime-equivalent roles.
  • Status: Proposed.

TD-004 — RLS policy catalog and FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY applicability

  • Problem statement: Tenant isolation requires consistent RLS/FORCE RLS posture, policy composition (restrictive tenant boundary and action/scope gates), and correct handling of SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/RETURNING semantics.
  • Security or correctness implications: Missing or miscomposed policies, owner bypass, or incorrect assumptions about UPDATE implying SELECT can leak cross-tenant data, block legitimate row-addressed operations, or permit unauthorized writes.
  • Available technical options:
    1. Verified-context-driven restrictive tenant policies plus permissive/action-scope gates on all tenant/protected tables, with FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY applied where ownership/role design permits and explicit UPDATE/SELECT/RETURNING design.
    2. Service-layer-only tenant filtering (no DB defense in depth).
    3. Coarse table-level RLS without action/scope composition (simpler, less expressive/precise).
  • Advantages and disadvantages:
    • Option 1: Pros: strongest alignment with reconciled security direction and fail-closed behavior. Cons: requires detailed policy catalog, testing, and careful privilege design.
    • Option 2: Pros: application simplicity. Cons: violates reconciled architecture and is unsafe.
    • Option 3: Pros: easier initial policy set. Cons: may not express required scope/action distinctions or evidence/licensing controls.
  • Recommended option, with technical justification: Option 1 (Proposed). Include explicit per-table/operation policy catalog, partition-table access controls, and a decision on whether approved write scopes imply required read visibility for row-addressed workflows.
  • Dependencies and assumptions: TD-001/TD-002/TD-003; table inventory and ownership model; approved scope vocabulary; PostgreSQL RLS/FORCE RLS behavior for selected version/roles.
  • Validation required: RLS allow/deny matrix tests, cross-tenant negative tests, FORCE RLS applicability checks, partition-parent/child behavior tests, UPDATE ... RETURNING/qualification visibility tests, and pooled-connection role tests.
  • Status: Proposed (includes owner/security decision on asset:write implying asset:read for approved row-addressed workflows).

TD-005 — Identity binding and fingerprint alias schema semantics

  • Problem statement: Source documents must use one reconciled identity model: canonical asset, stable source-device binding (asset_data_source/source_device_key_id), and versioned fingerprint aliases (source_device_fingerprint_alias), with explicit lookup/overlap/rotation/collision/migration semantics.
  • Security or correctness implications: Ambiguous identity/source-of-truth definitions can create duplicate bindings/assets/licensed usage, incorrect merges/splits, cross-tenant association errors, or broken fingerprint rotation/reprocessing.
  • Available technical options:
    1. Stable binding + separate versioned alias records with tenant-scoped uniqueness, overlap states, and deterministic lookup/conflict handling (reconciled direction).
    2. Fingerprint/key-version embedded as binding identity (rotation/overlap becomes identity rewrite risk).
    3. Connector-instance identity treated as device identity (incorrect for multi-device sources).
  • Advantages and disadvantages:
    • Option 1: Pros: preserves stable binding identity across rotation, supports overlap and auditable migration, aligns with ADR 0006/final corrections. Cons: more entities/constraints/transaction logic.
    • Option 2: Pros: fewer tables conceptually. Cons: conflicts with reconciled model; higher duplicate/collision/rotation risk.
    • Option 3: Pros: simplistic ingestion mapping. Cons: fundamentally unsafe for licensing correctness.
  • Recommended option, with technical justification: Option 1 (Proposed). Treat fingerprints/aliases as non-permanent lookup/verification material and stable binding identity as the continuity anchor.
  • Dependencies and assumptions: Protected fingerprint algorithm/key versioning and custody; connector/source-device key normalization rules; authoritative/weak/conflict evidence taxonomy; tenant-inclusive FK/uniqueness design; TD-006/TD-007 transaction/idempotency boundaries.
  • Validation required: Concurrency and correctness tests for same-identity registration, multi-source attachment, alias overlap/rotation, interrupted/resumed migration, collision/conflict handling, merge/split reassignment, and "no duplicate asset/binding/alias/licensed usage" invariants.
  • Status: Proposed.

TD-006 — Operation-by-operation transaction-boundary map

  • Problem statement: The reconciled architecture requires explicit atomicity for business state, idempotency/result, audit/lifecycle/licensing records, and outbox records, but operation boundaries are not fully specified across registration, attachment, merge, split, deactivation/reactivation/removal, fingerprint rotation, evidence transitions, and external-delivery workflows.
  • Security or correctness implications: Undefined boundaries create partial commits, duplicate side effects, lost audit/evidence linkage, counter/history divergence, and unsafe recovery after crashes/timeouts.
  • Available technical options:
    1. Explicit per-operation transaction matrix defining in-transaction artifacts, lock order, post-lock rechecks, commit outcomes, and compensating/reconciliation paths for out-of-transaction side effects.
    2. Best-effort application sequencing without formal boundary matrix (faster to draft, error-prone).
    3. Single generic transaction template for all operations (insufficient for differing external/evidence/replay semantics).
  • Advantages and disadvantages:
    • Option 1: Pros: reviewable correctness/security basis for schema and code; clarifies unknown-commit handling. Cons: requires detailed analysis and owner/security inputs.
    • Option 2: Pros: low upfront documentation effort. Cons: high implementation/review risk.
    • Option 3: Pros: simple mental model. Cons: ignores operation-specific invariants and external effects.
  • Recommended option, with technical justification: Option 1 (Proposed). Minimum required map should cover at least: registration/new asset, existing-asset attachment, pending identity creation/resolution, merge, split, deactivation, reactivation, removal/tombstone, fingerprint rotation/migration step, evidence controlled transition, ingestion acceptance, and outbox claim/reclaim/replay.
  • Dependencies and assumptions: TD-001–TD-005, TD-007–TD-009; approved state-to-counter mapping for owner-decided lifecycle semantics; provider/external side-effect characteristics.
  • Validation required: Failure-injection and unknown-commit tests per operation, rollback/atomicity verification, idempotent retry outcomes, concurrency/race tests, and reconciliation report correctness.
  • Status: Proposed.

TD-007 — Idempotency ledger scope and unknown-commit recovery

  • Problem statement: Reconciliation identified three distinct idempotency domains (ingestion receipts, licensing/identity operation ledger, outbox attempt/replay records) that must be consistently defined and durably persisted.
  • Security or correctness implications: Conflated or memory-only idempotency can cause duplicate assets/licensed usage, duplicate external side effects, lost acknowledgments, or inconsistent replay after timeouts/unknown commit outcomes.
  • Available technical options:
    1. Unified taxonomy with separate durable mechanisms per scope (event_receipt, licensing/identity operation idempotency ledger, outbox attempt/replay records), each with clear keys/state/result semantics.
    2. Single global idempotency table for all domains (possible but risks overloaded semantics and weaker constraints).
    3. Rely on request retries without durable result records (unsafe).
  • Advantages and disadvantages:
    • Option 1: Pros: matches reconciled documents, allows domain-specific uniqueness/atomicity rules, clearer recovery semantics. Cons: more schema objects and coordination rules.
    • Option 2: Pros: one storage location. Cons: complex polymorphic design; easy to blur correctness boundaries.
    • Option 3: Pros: minimal schema. Cons: unacceptable duplicate/ambiguity risk.
  • Recommended option, with technical justification: Option 1 (Proposed). Preserve event_receipt for ingestion acceptance, add durable tenant-scoped licensing/identity operation ledger per ADR 0006, and maintain outbox attempt/replay history per final corrections.
  • Dependencies and assumptions: TD-005/TD-006/TD-008; request canonicalization/hash strategy; retention windows (owner/security/operations decision); reconciliation tooling/process design.
  • Validation required: Duplicate same-payload retries, same-key different-payload conflicts, response-lost-after-commit recovery, concurrent duplicate submissions, replay after lifecycle transitions, and outbox/operation reconciliation tests.
  • Status: Proposed.

TD-008 — Outbox scope, delivery ambiguity, reconciliation, and replay

  • Problem statement: Event-processing outbox behavior and controlled external-side-effect/replay semantics are not fully harmonized. Final corrections define stricter attempt/generation/delivery_unknown handling that must be applied where appropriate.
  • Security or correctness implications: Ambiguous delivery handling without reconciliation/authorization can duplicate irreversible side effects, lose work, corrupt state transitions, or undermine auditability.
  • Available technical options:
    1. Two explicitly scoped outbox semantics/classes: lightweight event-processing outbox and controlled-delivery outbox with leases/fencing, cumulative attempts, generation-scoped replay controls, delivery_unknown, reconciliation evidence, and duplicate-risk authorization.
    2. Single outbox model with optional advanced fields for all messages (flexible but can be over-complex/misapplied).
    3. Synchronous external calls without durable outbox/replay state (poor resilience/recovery).
  • Advantages and disadvantages:
    • Option 1: Pros: aligns semantics to risk profile; preserves clarity for ingestion processing and strictness for ambiguous external side effects. Cons: requires clear classification rules and possibly separate schemas/workers.
    • Option 2: Pros: unified implementation substrate. Cons: risk of inconsistent use and harder validation.
    • Option 3: Pros: simple request flow. Cons: fails durability/retry/reconciliation needs.
  • Recommended option, with technical justification: Option 1 (Proposed), with shared primitives where safe. Apply final-corrections replay/ambiguity controls to workflows with external or non-idempotent/ambiguous side effects; keep event-processing idempotent and simpler but still durable and auditable.
  • Dependencies and assumptions: Provider/consumer idempotency capabilities and reconciliation evidence sources (owner/security/integration decision); TD-006/TD-007 boundaries; fencing/lease implementation; operational alerting/runbooks.
  • Validation required: Lease expiry/reclaim tests, duplicate worker claims, crash-before/after-send ambiguity cases, delivery_unknown reconciliation/replay authorization tests, generation-scoped attempt limits, and no exactly-once-external-delivery assumptions.
  • Status: Proposed.

TD-009 — Evidence storage metadata, custody, and controlled transitions

  • Problem statement: Forensic evidence handling requires reconciled metadata/custody/authorization semantics, but storage architecture and some lifecycle controls remain unresolved.
  • Security or correctness implications: Weak immutability/authorization or ambiguous custody handling can compromise evidentiary integrity, tenant isolation, legal defensibility, and auditability.
  • Available technical options:
    1. DB-managed immutable evidence metadata + append-only custody events + protected transaction-bound controlled-transition authorization, with evidence objects in approved storage and hash verification (reconciled direction).
    2. Application-only evidence state management (bypassable and hard to audit).
    3. Full external evidence system dependency before core controls are designed (premature coupling; still needs CARES authorization/metadata model).
  • Advantages and disadvantages:
    • Option 1: Pros: aligns with SECURITY_ARCHITECTURE and final corrections; clear tenant-scoped integrity model and controlled transitions. Cons: requires careful schema/procedure/role design and storage integration decisions.
    • Option 2: Pros: minimal DB complexity. Cons: insufficient integrity and privilege separation.
    • Option 3: Pros: may leverage specialized tooling. Cons: external dependency/approval risk; does not replace core authorization/custody semantics.
  • Recommended option, with technical justification: Option 1 (Proposed). Use database-enforced metadata/custody/authorization boundaries as designed, and treat external immutable/WORM storage as an additional approved control rather than a substitute for correct DB authorization semantics.
  • Dependencies and assumptions: TD-001–TD-004; evidence object storage design; retention/legal-hold/purge approvals; hash algorithm/provenance standards; operational procedures for verification/restore/reconciliation.
  • Validation required: Immutability trigger/policy tests (IS DISTINCT FROM coverage), controlled-transition negative tests (including no-GUC-authorization), custody sequence/hash-chain concurrency tests, atomic authorization consume/update/custody append behavior, rollback/replay resistance, and integrity verification workflows.
  • Status: Proposed.

Cross-cutting dependencies and assumptions

  • Dependencies: TD-001–TD-004 underpin tenant isolation, verified context, and protected controlled procedures; TD-005–TD-007 underpin licensing/identity correctness; TD-008/TD-009 depend on transaction boundaries and role/authorization design.
  • Assumptions (unresolved): selected PostgreSQL version/features; assertion cryptography/key management; pooling/session behavior; provider reconciliation/idempotency contracts; approved lifecycle/state-to-counter mappings; storage/retention/legal-hold architecture; representative workload/benchmark environment.
  • Constraint preservation: Python backend, PostgreSQL authoritative system of record, one unique monitored device = one licensed asset, multi-source no-duplicate-licensed-asset rule, asset licensing separate from technical resource quotas, external SaaS AI only/no local GPU, core independent of MELIRA, and original roadmap/commercial decisions preserved.

Readiness note (technical decision preparation)

This document prepares technical options and proposed recommendations but does not make the architecture schema-ready by itself. Formal PostgreSQL schema design should proceed only after reconciling source-document terminology/mechanisms per the review/changelog and resolving or explicitly tracking the required technical selections and owner decisions above. All recommendations remain Proposed/NOT IMPLEMENTED/NOT TESTED.
